question: What is the main substance that moves across the cell membrane during osmosis?
explanation: Osmosis describes the movement of solvent molecules, specifically water, across a selectively permeable membrane. [learn more](BMP111_U1_T4#BMP111_U1_T4_h1)

question: Why does osmosis not require the cell to spend energy?

options.A: It uses special pumps built directly into the phospholipid bilayer
options.B: It only happens when the cell is resting and producing excess energy
options.C: It relies on the natural kinetic energy of water molecules moving down a gradient
options.D: It forces solutes to move against their natural concentration gradient

explanation: Because water moves passively along its concentration gradient during osmosis, no cellular energy expenditure is needed. [learn more](BMP111_U1_T4#BMP111_U1_T4_h1)

question: Which of the following describes the main feature of a selectively permeable cell membrane?

options.A: It allows every type of molecule to move freely in both directions
options.B: It actively pushes large protein structures out of the cytoplasm
options.C: It prevents all liquids and gases from entering the cell
options.D: It lets some substances pass through while blocking others

explanation: A selectively permeable membrane acts as a barrier, permitting certain molecules to cross while restricting others. [learn more](BMP111_U1_T4#BMP111_U1_T4_h2)

question: What happens if a solute is too large to pass through the cell membrane?

options.A: The cell membrane dissolves to let the large solute pass freely
options.B: The solute breaks down into smaller gas molecules instantly
options.C: Water moves across the membrane instead to balance the concentration
options.D: Active transport immediately stops working inside the cytoplasm

explanation: When solutes cannot cross the barrier, water shifts across the membrane to equalize the concentration differences on both sides. [learn more](BMP111_U1_T4#BMP111_U1_T4_h2)

question: In what direction do water molecules move during osmosis?

options.A: From low water concentration to high water concentration
options.B: From high water concentration to low water concentration
options.C: From inside the blood vessels straight out to the bones
options.D: From areas of high pressure to areas of low temperature

explanation: Water naturally travels down its concentration gradient, flowing where it is most abundant to where it is less abundant. [learn more](BMP111_U1_T4#BMP111_U1_T4_h3)

question: How is the concentration of water related to the concentration of solutes in a given fluid?

options.A: Solute and water concentrations always increase together
options.B: Higher solute concentration means higher water concentration
options.C: Higher solute concentration means lower water concentration
options.D: There is no relationship between them

explanation: When more solutes are dissolved in a solution, they take up space, leaving fewer water molecules per unit of volume. [learn more](BMP111_U1_T4#BMP111_U1_T4_h3)

question: Which type of solution causes water to rush into a cell because the surrounding fluid has fewer solutes?
explanation: In a hypotonic solution, the external environment has a lower solute concentration, so water enters the cell to balance things out. [learn more](BMP111_U1_T4#BMP111_U1_T4_h4)

question: What happens to the movement of water when a living cell is placed in an isotonic solution?

options.A: Water stops moving across the cell membrane entirely
options.B: Water moves rapidly out of the cell, causing it to shrivel completely
options.C: Water moves in and out at equal rates, so cell shape remains stable
options.D: Water rushes into the cell until the outer cell membrane bursts

explanation: An isotonic solution matches the internal solute level, so water enters and leaves the cell at the exact same rate. [learn more](BMP111_U1_T4#BMP111_U1_T4_h4)

question: What term describes the bursting of a red blood cell when placed in a very hypotonic solution?
explanation: Hemolysis refers to the rupture of red blood cells caused by excessive water entry in a hypotonic environment. [learn more](BMP111_U1_T4#BMP111_U1_T4_h5)

question: Why does a red blood cell undergo crenation when placed in a hypertonic solution?

options.A: Water rushes inside the cell until the plasma membrane stretches apart
options.B: Water flows out of the cell into the surrounding hypertonic liquid
options.C: Solutes from the outside environment enter the cytoplasm to cause swelling
options.D: Cellular proteins actively pump out all remaining internal water molecules

explanation: Hypertonic surroundings draw water out of the red blood cell, causing it to shrink and wrinkle up. [learn more](BMP111_U1_T4#BMP111_U1_T4_h5)

question: Why are isotonic intravenous fluids commonly used to treat dehydration in clinical practice?

options.A: They restore fluid balance without causing abnormal swelling or shrinking of blood cells
options.B: They prevent all forms of passive transport from occurring inside the kidneys
options.C: They instantly convert excess body fat into usable water and energy
options.D: They actively pump extra electrolytes directly into the bones

explanation: Isotonic fluids match body fluid tonicity, allowing safe rehydration without triggering harmful osmotic shifts in blood cells. [learn more](BMP111_U1_T4#BMP111_U1_T4_h6)

question: Which of the following is NOT a clinical risk of giving an inappropriate fluid tonicity to a patient?

options.A: Severe fluid imbalance within the vascular and cellular compartments
options.B: Immediate strengthening of the cell walls across all body tissues
options.C: Dangerous swelling and rupture of circulating red blood cells
options.D: Excessive shrinkage of cells due to fluid loss into surrounding spaces

explanation: Giving incorrect IV fluid tonicity causes cell damage like hemolysis or crenation, not strengthening. [learn more](BMP111_U1_T4#BMP111_U1_T4_h6)
